To the edge of what we know

From the Sun to a photographed black hole. Leaving brings you back to Earth.

Open the trip: To the edge of what we know

The Sun, from one light-year

From here the whole Solar System is smaller than a pixel. Light from the Sun takes a year to reach this spot; Voyager 1, the fastest thing we have sent out of the Solar System, would take about eighteen thousand.

Proxima Centauri

The nearest star to the Sun, a dim red one an eighth of the Sun's mass. It has at least one planet. Every star you can see with your eyes at night is farther away than this one.

Sirius

The brightest star in our sky, eight and a half light-years out and twenty-five times as bright as the Sun. The light reaching your eye tonight left it eight and a half years ago.

The Pleiades

Over a thousand young stars, a hundred million years old, about four hundred and twenty-five light-years away. Their light left when Shakespeare was alive.

The centre of the galaxy

Twenty-seven thousand light-years from home, a black hole of four million Suns that the whole Milky Way turns around. The disc, bar and arms drawn around you are a model built from measurements; the stars are the measured part.

The Milky Way

Our galaxy, about ninety thousand light-years across, seen from sixty thousand light-years above its disc, a view nobody has had. The shape is an illustration of what has been measured.

Andromeda

The nearest big galaxy, two and a half million light-years away and coming our way. Its light left when the first humans were learning to use tools.

As far as this trip goes

Fifty-three million light-years: the black hole in M87, the first one ever photographed. The map goes further, to a quasar's black hole 18.3 billion light-years out, whose light left 10.8 billion years ago. It shows 109 389 stars of the 1.8 billion Gaia has measured, 209 nebulae, clusters and galaxies (110 of them from OpenNGC's 13 372), and every confirmed planet around another star whose distance has been measured. The rest is out there; we have not drawn what we cannot place.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
